name: Hit the Road Dude AI
tagline: Uploads one photo and renders a short AI video of a private-property confrontation meme, with six canned scene options.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as prepaid credit packs with optional subscriptions, entry pack reportedly around USD 9.90.

verdictSummary: The product itself is a thin, pleasant shell: upload a photo, pick one of six prompt presets, watch a preview, download an MP4. An agent can rebuild that shell in an afternoon, including the preset library and a local output folder, because none of it is hard. What it cannot rebuild is the image-to-video model doing the actual work, so your clone points at fal.ai or Replicate and you swap credit packs for metered API bills. That is a real dependency, not a moat you crossed, and per-render cost may land close to what the packs charge. Note also what neither version gives you: the original meme audio, guaranteed dialogue, lip sync, or a likeness that actually resembles the person in the photo.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that takes one uploaded photo, applies one of six hardcoded scene prompts, calls a hosted image-to-video endpoint, and saves the result to disk with a preview player.
requirements: An API key for a hosted image-to-video model such as fal.ai or Replicate, billed per render
Optionally a local GPU with 16GB or more VRAM if you want to run Wan or SVD yourself instead
ffmpeg if you want to lay your own audio over the output
whatYouLose: Prompt presets that someone already tuned against the model, which is most of the actual craft here
A hosted queue that absorbs long render times and retries failures instead of leaving you staring at a terminal
Any pretense of cost predictability: credit packs cap your spend, a raw API key does not
Mobile-friendly uploading and sharing that works from a phone without you running a dev server
A legal buffer, thin as it is, between you and the likeness or meme-source questions your renders raise
moatNotes: The GPU time is the product and it is rented, not owned. The differentiator is prompt tuning and a clean upload-to-download path, both of which are copyable.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because USD 9.90 for a handful of renders is cheaper than an afternoon of your time plus the inevitable discovery that your own prompts produce a melted face holding a shotgun-shaped smear. The presets are the value: someone sat there burning credits until six scenes reliably came out watchable, and you are buying that search, not the software. People also pay because the whole thing is an impulse purchase for one joke sent to one group chat, and nobody provisions an API key for a single joke.
notes: A preset library in a trench coat, which is not an insult: the presets are the only part that took work.
prompt:
Build a local single-user image-to-video meme renderer in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS. No database, no auth, no accounts, no analytics, no telemetry. Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost only.

In scope:
- A single page with a drag-and-drop photo upload (jpg/png, max 10MB), client-side preview of the uploaded still.
- A `scenes.ts` config exporting six scene presets. Each preset: id, label, one-sentence description shown in the UI, and a full text prompt for the video model. Write six plausible presets for a confrontational front-yard "this is private property" bit: porch warning, driveway standoff, fence-line shouting, mailbox lecture, hose threat, slow walk-away. Keep the prompt text in one place so it is trivial to tune.
- A server route POST /api/render that takes the image plus a scene id, calls a hosted image-to-video endpoint (default: fal.ai image-to-video, key from FAL_KEY in .env.local), polls until done, downloads the MP4 into ./outputs/, and writes a sibling .json with timestamp, scene id, prompt used, and reported cost if the API returns one.
- A gallery route reading ./outputs/ that lists past renders newest first with an inline HTML5 video player and a download link.
- An optional POST /api/mux that runs local ffmpeg to overlay an audio file the user drops in ./audio/ onto a chosen render. Skip gracefully with a clear message if ffmpeg is not on PATH.

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, credit systems, payment, sharing links, cloud storage, mobile app, queue workers, a model of your own.

Requirements: secrets only in .env.local, committed .env.example, a README stating plainly that renders cost real money per call, that the model may ignore the prompt, and that lip sync, dialogue and likeness are not guaranteed. Print the per-render API cost to the console after each job. Fail loudly with the raw API error instead of swallowing it.
